'''Norman C. Deno''' (February 15, 1921 – September 22, 2017) was an American [[Chemistry|chemist]] and [[plant scientist]]. He was a professor of chemistry at [[Penn State University]] and is known as one of the foremost researchers in [[seed germination]] theory. He researched the biochemical reactions that underlie the germination of all seeds, performing germination research on plant species from 150 families, 800 genera, and 2500 species over the course of his career. Deno authored 150 papers in chemistry and 20 papers in [[horticulture]], and self-published a number of books that combined his scientific results.

A [[Chicagoan]], Deno had an interest in plants from a young age, but obtained a [[post-doctoral degree]] in chemistry as a more lucrative career opportunity. His chemistry professor position at Penn State University resulted in a discovery by his lab on coal refinement for [[oil refineries]] that earned him a large amount of wealth from grants. He later reduced his focus on chemistry to pursue his interests in horticulture. Determining the germination requirements for plants had Deno create the "baggie and paper towel" method for mimicking laboratory growth settings and his general low tech methodologies would end up being dubbed "The Deno Method". His approach to seed germination would result in multiple interviews in newspapers and for books, along with seed companies coming to him specifically for specific cultivar research. He went on to publish multiple books covering seed germination theory and he received awards from the [[North American Rock Garden Society]] for his work.

==Childhood and education==
Born in Chicago on February 15, 1921,<ref name="CDT Obituary"/> Deno suffered from [[asthma]] as a child and was unable to participate in outdoor sports in school. Instead, he focused on growing plants and became acquainted with [[daylily]] hybrid expert [[David F. Hall]] who further increased Deno's interest in plant biology.<ref>{{cite news |last=Frankel |first=Tamara |date=July 20, 1985 |title=Retired professor cherishes gardening |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/92476047/retired-professor-cherishes-gardening/ |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |access-date=January 12, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> He began giving presentations at [[garden clubs]] at 13, but also became interested in the chemistry of [[fireworks]] alongside his father.<ref name="Avocation"/>

His teenage years during the [[Great Depression]] saw hard times for his family and, since there was little income to be made in the field of [[horticulture]] despite his interest in the subject, he chose to study chemistry at the [[University of Illinois]], where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in 1942.<ref name="Avocation"/> He earned a Master of Science degree in chemistry and a Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1946 and 1948.<ref>{{cite book |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=American Men & Women of Science : A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological and Related Sciences |chapter=Deno, Norman C |url=https://library.princeton.edu/resource/4649 |publisher=[[Gale (publisher)|Gale]] |volume=4 |page=2576 |date=2019}}</ref> During his research for his doctoral degree, he focused on studying the chemistry of explosives in relation to munitions used in [[World War II]]. From 1942 to 1946, he studied under [[Werner Emmanuel Bachmann]] on the production of the explosive [[RDX]] in order to reduce the likelihood of premature detonation during handling for use in [[torpedoes]].<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=September 27, 1972 |title=Explosive Developer: a Saintly Man |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107082262/explosive-developer-a-saintly-man/ |work=[[Standard-Speaker]] |access-date=August 6, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=November 19, 1962 |title=Chem. Society Holds Meeting |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/107082305/chem-society-holds-meeting/ |work=[[The Danville News]] |access-date=August 6, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> After his graduate work, he completed a post-doctoral research degree at [[Ohio University]].<ref name="Avocation"/>

==Career and research==
===Chemistry (1950–1980)===
After graduating, Deno moved to [[State College, Pennsylvania]] and became a professor of chemistry at Penn State University in 1950.<ref name="CDT Obituary"/> During his time as a chemist, Deno and his lab students discovered a new technique for the chemical characterization of [[coal deposit]]s.  

Chemists had long been able to distinguish [[aromatic (chemistry)|aromatic]] moieties in coal through [[dealkylation]] reactions followed by [[distillation]],<ref name=Pyrite/>{{rp|pp=3-7,10}} but the aliphatic sidechains remained relatively undifferentiated.<ref name=CPR/><!--<ref name=Pyrite/> discusses a solvent extraction process, but it only captures the low-molecular weight fractions.-->  Deno's lab claimed to demonstrate that a mixture of [[trifluoroacetic acid]] and [[hydrogen peroxide]] would selectively oxidize the aromatic portions of the coal, leaving functionalized aliphates amenable to characterization.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/0016-2361(80)90021-6|title=Dihydroaromatic structure of Illinois No. 6 Monterey coal|first1=N. C.|last1=Deno|first2=Kenneth W.|last2=Curry|first3=Barbara A.|last3=Greigger|first4=A. Daniel|last4=Jones|first5=Walter G.|last5=Rakitsky|first6=Karen Ann|last6=Smith|first7=Karen|last7=Wagner|first8=Robert D.|last8=Minard|orig-date=6 Nov 1979|publisher=IPC Business Press|date=Oct 1980|journal=Fuel|volume=59}}</ref>  The resulting process would, in principle, reduce the amount necessary to determine if the deposit suited [[oil refinery]] customers from 20&nbsp;tons to less than 1&nbsp;gram.<ref name=CPR>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=June 2, 1980 |title=New Process To Make Coal Selection Easier |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/92474618/new-process-to-make-coal-selection/ |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |access-date=January 12, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>  

Excited by the process, Occidental Petroleum Research Corporation granted Deno funds to investigate the method further,<ref name=CPR/> and later Deno would say that "as a chemist he made a considerable impact&nbsp;&mdash; and money&nbsp;&mdash; with a finding relating to the operation of oil refineries."<ref name="Fisher"/>{{rp|7}}  But Deno quickly changed his research focus to biology,<ref name=Avocation/> and by 1984 it had become clear that Deno oxidation could not be controlled in the presence of [[iron pyrite]], a common coal impurity.<ref name=Pyrite>{{cite thesis|url=https://digitalcommons.wku.edu/theses/2709|institution=[[Western Kentucky University]]|date=19 April 1984|title=H2O2-TFA-H2SO4 Oxidation of Coal & Coal Model Compounds|first=Darrell|last=Pierce|via=TopSCHOLAR|type=MA}}</ref>{{rp|pp=48,55}}  
<!--Further details: a quick Google Scholar search turns up DOIs 10.1016/0016-2361(84)90223-0 and 10.1016/0016-2361(88)90260-8, suggesting that (respectively) the Ruhr and India could not replicate his results.  The only examples I could find using the method appear in 10.1016/0016-2361(92)90028-M, which says that "The TFPA reagent was first applied to coals by Deno et al. in 1978 and since that time has been used extensively for the selective degradation of coals", with cites to 10.1016/0016-2361(82)90190-9 (Appalachia) and 10.1016/0016-7037(85)90265-0 (Australia) that seem legit.  I asked Copilot Deep Research whether the method had seen industrial application and it was unable to turn up any other (!) discussion treating the technique favorably, but plenty of stuff (including the Pierce thesisin <ref name=Pyrite/>) showing it irreproducible.-->

===Horticulture (1980–2017)===
He retired from the position in 1980 to focus on his personal hobby research in horticulture and specifically the chemical processes involved in the seed germination process..<ref name="Avocation">{{cite news |last=Terenzini |first=Caroline |date=February 28, 1995 |title='Avocation' plants seeds of study |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/92470595/avocation-plants-seeds-of-study/ |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |access-date=January 12, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> A large amount of his research proved useful for gardeners and those wanting to successfully germinate specific species of plants outside of a lab setting. He found that almost all of the plants he studied used chemicals to determine the timing of germination, which included his studies on the plant hormone [[gibberellic acid]] that increases germination rates. He also researched how germination could be manipulated artificially through both physical and chemical means by creating the "baggie and paper towel" method, which uses temperature control and moisture to provoke germination.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gruenhagen |first1=Gary |name-list-style=vanc |date=December 2015 |title=The Virtual Gardener — The Science of Seeds |url=https://cals.arizona.edu/cochise/mg/sites/cals.arizona.edu.cochise.mg/files/newsletter/Dec15.pdf |journal=High on the Desert Cochise County Master Gardener Newsletter |publisher=University of Arizona and U.S. Department of Agriculture Cooperating |volume=26 |issue=12 |pages=1–2 |access-date=February 13, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Love |first1=Stephen |last2=Akins |first2=Candace |date=Fall 2019 |title=Fourth summary of the native seed germination studies of Norman C Deno: species with names beginning with letters L through O |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/746689 |journal=[[Native Plants Journal]] |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=279–304 |doi=10.3368/npj.20.3.279 |s2cid=258100005 |access-date=February 12, 2021 |name-list-style=vanc|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

His contributions to the [[North American Rock Garden Society]] helped promote this method and his technique requiring simple household items for accomplishing germination was referred to as "The Deno Method". This involved replicating the lab setting of [[blotting paper]] for sowing seeds and the use of germination chambers by instead using heavy-duty paper towels and plastic sandwich bags to imitate the enclosed chamber environment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Maroni |first1=Donna |date=January–February 1998 |title=Seeds, Dr. Deno And Me |url=https://florapix.nl/arisaema-l/secure/Literature/Maroni%20-%20Seeds,%20Dr.%20Deno%20and%20me.pdf |journal=The Trillium |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=11–15 |access-date=February 13, 2021 |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>

For his other horticultural research, Deno argued that the term "[[drainage]]" in regards to watering of plants is fundamentally wrong, as it does not matter the amount of flowing level of water over the roots, but the amount of contained oxygen in them and the capability of the plant at that growth stage to uptake the oxygen into the plant body. He suggested all usage of the term drainage should be replaced with [[Water aeration|aeration]] for accuracy.<ref name="Fisher"/>

From his understanding of chemical responses boosting germination, he suggested that the idea of [[seed dormancy]] is inaccurate, as there is no form of hibernation going on. The seeds are still active and so he prefers the term "conditioning" in that the seeds are waiting for chemical signals to show that the outside conditions are right so their activity can proceed beyond the [[seed coat]].<ref name="Fisher">{{cite magazine |last=Fisher |first=Kathleen |date=January 1994 |title=A Fresh Look At Seeds |url=https://ahsgardening.org/wp-content/pdfs/1994-01r.pdf |magazine=[[American Horticulturist]] |publisher=[[American Horticultural Society]] |volume=73 |issue=1 |access-date=February 13, 2021 |pages=6–7}}</ref> Deno stressed that sterilized soil had to be used in order to prevent encroachment of [[pathogenic fungi]].<ref>{{cite news |last=St. Marie |first=Jim |date=February 5, 1994 |title=Sterilize soil before planting seeds |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/275298624 |work=[[Waterloo Region Record]] |pages=D8 |id={{ProQuest|275298624}}}}</ref>

These methodologies developed by Deno were reproduced by gardening photographer [[Ken Druse]] for his book ''Making More Plants: The Science, Art and Joy of Propagation''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Raver |first=Anne |date=January 14, 2001 |title=Need for more plants leads to book about propagation |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/271793739 |work=[[The San Diego Union-Tribune]] |page=I-29 |id={{ProQuest|271793739}}}}</ref> Seed companies sought his expertise in finding germination techniques for their products; [[Thompson & Morgan]] incorporated his methods into their customer directions.<ref name="Hugo">{{cite news |last=Hugo |first=Nancy Ross |date=January 10, 1998 |title=Exposing The Secret Life Of Seeds |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/423665169 |work=[[Richmond Times-Dispatch]] |page=E1-E6 |id={{ProQuest|423665169}}}}</ref> He received an Award of Merit in 1978 for his contributions to gardening and a Carleton R. Worth Award in 1990 for his horticultural publications from the North American Rock Garden Society.<ref name="CDT Obituary">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |title=Norman C. Deno Obituary |url=https://nargs.org/news/2017-09-24/norman-c-deno-obituary |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |date=September 24, 2017 |access-date=February 13, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=June 2, 1978 |title=Rock Garden Award Goes to Dr. Deno |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/92476935/rock-garden-award-goes-to-dr-deno/ |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |access-date=January 12, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

===Books===
In the early 1980's, Deno decided to write a companion book to horticulturalist and [[plant taxonomist]] [[Bernard Emerson Harkness]]'s ''Seedlist Handbook'', which was a reference book on plant characteristics for seed exchanges between expert growers. Deno's book was to focus on seed germination techniques and the requirements and needs of different species, a topic he felt was lacking from Harkness' and others' works.<ref name="Avocation"/>

The first volume he self-published was titled ''Seed Germination Theory and Practice'' and has been referred to by ''Alpine Gardening'' as "the bible" of horticulture and a required book for gardeners and those who work with plants.<ref name="Kerstetter">{{cite news |last=Kerstetter |first=Rich |date=May 8, 2003 |title=Growing Pains |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/92473927/growing-pains/ |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |access-date=January 12, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Original physical copies were sold by Deno for $20 through the mail and he estimated that over 40,000 copies were bought in total.<ref name="Kerstetter"/><ref>{{cite news |last=Rogers |first=Paul |date=November 20, 1997 |title=Plant propagation is well worth studying |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/268664710 |work=[[Telegram & Gazette]] |id={{ProQuest|268664710}}}}</ref> The second edition of the book was published in 1993 and listed germination rules for over 2,500 individual species of plants. These covered 605 different [[genera]] of plants. The first supplement to the book was published in 1996 and added 1,080 further species.<ref name="Hugo"/><ref>{{cite news |last=Benet |first=James |date=August 26, 1992 |title=From Little Seeds a Passion Grows |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/303076104 |work=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |page=4/Z3 |id={{ProQuest|303076104}}}}</ref> A final volume of his research that was to be titled "Seed Storage Theory and Practice" was never written.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.reeves-reedarboretum.org/blogs/detail.php?What-Every-Seed-Knows-55 |title=What Every Seed Knows |last=Montefusco |first=Marc |date=February 15, 2019 |website=[[Reeves-Reed Arboretum]] |access-date=February 12, 2021}}</ref> In total, his book and supplements covered germination research on plant species from 150 families, 800 genera, and 2500 species.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Love |first1=Stephen |last2=Akins |first2=Candace |date=Spring 2020 |title=Fifth summary of the native seed germination studies of Norman C Deno: species with names beginning with letters P and Q |url=http://npj.uwpress.org/content/21/1/83.short |journal=[[Native Plants Journal]] |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=83–111 |doi=10.3368/npj.21.1.83 |s2cid=241374952 |access-date=February 12, 2021 |name-list-style=vanc|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Copies of Deno's works are hosted in the [[United States National Agricultural Library]] archive.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://naldc-legacy.nal.usda.gov/naldc/catalog.xhtml?id=41278 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190315003338/https://naldc-legacy.nal.usda.gov/naldc/catalog.xhtml?id=41278 |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 15, 2019 |title=NALDC Record Details: Seed germination, theory and practice |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=February 2019 |website=[[National Agricultural Library]] |publisher=[[USDA]] |access-date=February 13, 2021}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Deno had three children with his wife Ginny before her death after 52 years of marriage. He met his second wife Janet at a [[ballroom dancing]] event. They married in 1997 and remained together until his death on September 22, 2017.<ref name="CDT Obituary"/>

He was a lifetime member of the North American Rock Garden Society, the [[Alpine Garden Society]], and the [[Scottish Rock Garden Club]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Schumacher |first=Jerilynn |date=March 1, 1998 |title=Winter garden |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/92477172/winter-garden/ |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |access-date=January 12, 2022 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>
